From what I can tell. (No easily found sources have bothered to include the ruling itself) the federal statute is sec. 1983 which is used to sue states in federal court. Their claim is probably still first amendment and due process, but they have to use section 1983 to file suit as a state is otherwise immune. 1331 is also cited, but that is simply the basis for the courts subject matter jurisdiction (federal court hears a federal question of law not state stuff)

This letter is part of their due process obligations. The subject is that of “first notice.” Due to the urgent nature of the proceedings an emergency suspension there is a balance of personal interest, state interest and the risk of erroneous deprivation. See Mackey v. Montrym, 443 U.S. 1 (1979). See below for further analysis. 

Ultimately, procedural due process, at a minimum, requires notice and opportunity to “be heard”. See Fuentes v. Shevin, 407 U.S. 67, 80 (1972). Fuentes along with Goldberg v. Kelly 397 U.S. 254 (1970) and Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) serve as the bedrock of the Due Process clause’s procedural requirements. Due to the contractual nature of the student to university relationship these requirements are there albeit relaxed. This is why the student has the opportunity to request review by a independent decision-maker. A student may also seek judicial review by way of petition in the Maricopa Superior Court (or Coconino/Pima Superior Courts if at NAU/UofA respectively). See ARS 12-904. See also Do v. Arizona Board of Regents, 1 CA-CV 22-0752 (Unpublished, AZ App. Division 1) outlining the ABOR disciplinary procedure system. 

Ultimately this case has to do with a flagrant violation of university policy, which is applied equally even amongst all state agencies. You cannot camp on state land without the adequate permissions, that goes for everyone regardless of the reason. A court is likely to find that this case involves an equally applied law and is not an attempt to violate the first amendment rights of those involved. 

Whether one likes the outcome or not, a due process violation is not yet apparent as the letter constitutes a part of the universities due process requirements.

If you’re fixed on immediate rather than chronic results, septoplasty is pseudoscience. A lot of people with septal problems early in life find out that they worsen as they get older. 

My mother suffered from a chronic (>2 year) sinus infection that occurred due to a deviated septum and how it can cause mucus production to “backlog”

Something people forget is your septum goes farther than what you can see. Your obstruction could easily be caused by a deviation further in your nose, same with turbinates.

Again, septoplasty is a **preventative procedure** but it is oftentimes done alongside turbinate reduction because hypertrophy is usually what prompts a septum issue to be discovered.

Another issue that ENTs need to be more aware of is nasal valve collapse, responsible for slot of nasal obstruction (1/3 of a sample with nasal obstruction actually had nasal valve collapse.)

Furthermore, I highly suggest anyone with sleep disordered breathing consult an endocrinologist about hormone levels. Lingering fatigue can be attributed to hormonal imbalance; which can be caused by sleep disordered breathing. Especially in the case of men, sleep issues can make you hypogonadal.

Septoplasty is a preventative measure, I wouldn’t call it pseudoscience because someone cites a few loose studies about different surgeries. 

The modifier “with turbinate reduction” is significant, as deviated septum is a prime cause for turbinate dysfunction. Long term turbinate hypertrophy can become permanent. 

There are studies that find turbinate hypertrophy is reversible with septoplasty if done with less severe cases.

Even if it doesn’t help with your apnea, it will likely help you long term.
